modules.title: Budgeting & Cash Flow
modules.subtitle: Take control of where your money goes

lessons.title: Why Budgeting Works
lessons.summary: The mindset and math behind a budget.

blocks.text: Why Budgeting Works
A budget is simply a plan for your money before the month begins. Without one, money leaks out through dozens of small, forgettable decisions. With one, every rupee has a job.

items: A budget is permission to spend, not a restriction
Track for 30 days before optimising
Pay yourself first: save before you spend

items.def: All money you receive in a period
Same every month: rent, EMI, subscriptions
Changes monthly: food, fuel, shopping
Wants you can pause: dining out, gadgets

blocks.text: Track every expense for one month. You cannot improve what you don't measure.
blocks.title: First action

opts: Save before spending on anything else
items.explain: Automating savings before you spend protects your goals.
Rent is the same each month, so it's fixed.

lessons.title: The 50/30/20 Rule
lessons.summary: A simple split that fits most incomes.

blocks.text: The 50/30/20 Rule
Divide your post-tax income into three buckets. It's not perfect, but it's a fast, durable default.
If 50% can't cover your needs, your fixed costs are too high — attack the biggest one first (usually rent or EMIs).

blocks.q: On a take-home of 50,000, how much should go to savings under 50/30/20?

blocks.text: Zero-Based Budgeting
Income minus expenses minus savings should equal exactly zero. Every rupee is assigned, so nothing drifts away unnoticed.

steps.title: List income
steps.body: Total all take-home pay for the month.

steps.title: Assign categories
steps.body: Allocate down to needs, wants, savings.

steps.title: Adjust weekly
steps.body: Move money between categories as life happens.

items.a: Only the first month. After that you copy last month and tweak.
Budget on your lowest expected month; treat extra as a bonus to save.

blocks.text: Building an Emergency Fund
An emergency fund is cash set aside for true emergencies — job loss, medical bills, urgent repairs. It keeps you out of high-interest debt.

items: Target 3–6 months of essential expenses
Keep it liquid: savings account or liquid fund
Start with a 25,000 mini-fund, then grow it

blocks.text: An emergency fund is insurance, not an investment. Its job is to be boring and available.
blocks.title: Mindset

blocks.q: How many months of essential expenses should an emergency fund cover?
blocks.explain: 3–6 months is the standard guidance for most people.

lessons.title: Simple vs Compound Interest
lessons.summary: The most important idea in finance.

blocks.text: Simple vs Compound Interest
Simple interest is earned only on your principal. Compound interest is earned on principal plus all previously earned interest — interest on interest.
Over 20 years, compounding more than doubles the simple-interest result. Time is the key ingredient.
blocks.title: The magic

items.explain: That 'interest on interest' is what compounds.

items.q: What single factor most amplifies compounding?
items.explain: The longer money compounds, the more dramatic the growth.

lessons.title: The Rule of 72
lessons.summary: Estimate doubling time in your head.

blocks.text: The Rule of 72
Divide 72 by the annual return to estimate how many years it takes your money to double.

blocks.q: At 9% annual return, roughly how long to double your money?

blocks.text: Inflation: The Silent Tax
Inflation is the rise in prices over time. At 6% inflation, money loses about half its purchasing power in 12 years.
If your savings account pays 3% and inflation is 6%, you are losing 3% of purchasing power every year by staying in cash.

blocks.q: Savings pays 4%, inflation is 7%. Your real return is…

modules.title: Investing Foundations
modules.subtitle: Put your money to work for the long run

lessons.title: Risk and Return
lessons.summary: Why higher returns demand higher risk.

blocks.text: Risk and Return
Return is the reward; risk is the uncertainty of that reward. There is no free lunch — durable higher returns require accepting more volatility.

items.def: How much a price swings up and down
Peak-to-trough drop in value
How fast you can sell at fair price
Extra return for taking on risk

opts: Extra return for taking on risk
items.explain: Investors demand extra return to bear extra risk.

lessons.title: Diversification
lessons.summary: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.

blocks.text: Diversification
Spreading money across many assets reduces the impact of any single one failing. It's the closest thing to a free lunch in investing.

items: Diversify across assets, sectors, and geographies
An index fund instantly diversifies across hundreds of stocks
Diversification reduces risk without necessarily reducing return

blocks.text: Correlation matters: assets that fall together don't diversify. Mix things that behave differently.
blocks.title: Nuance

blocks.q: The main benefit of diversification is…
opts: Lower risk from any single failure
blocks.explain: It reduces the damage any one holding can do.

blocks.text: Rupee-Cost Averaging (SIP)
Investing a fixed amount on a schedule buys more units when prices are low and fewer when high, smoothing your average cost and removing the need to time the market.

steps.title: Pick an amount
steps.body: Choose a monthly amount you won't miss.

steps.title: Automate it
steps.body: Set an auto-debit SIP into an index fund.

steps.title: Stay consistent
steps.body: Keep investing through ups and downs.

steps.title: Increase yearly
steps.body: Step up the amount as income grows.

blocks.latex: Avg cost = Total invested / Total units bought

blocks.back: Systematic Investment Plan — fixed amount invested on a schedule

lessons.title: Asset Allocation
lessons.summary: The decision that drives most returns.

blocks.text: Asset Allocation
Asset allocation is how you split money across stocks, bonds, and cash. Studies show it explains the majority of a portfolio's long-term result — far more than individual stock picking.
A classic rough rule: equity % ≈ 100 minus your age. Adjust for your own risk tolerance and goals.

items.explain: It's the mix of asset classes.

items.q: A 30-year-old using the '100 minus age' rule targets what equity %?

modules.title: Stock Market Basics

lessons.title: What Is a Stock?
lessons.summary: Owning a slice of a business.

blocks.text: What Is a Stock?
A stock (or share) is a unit of ownership in a company. Own one share and you own a tiny fraction of the entire business — its assets, profits, and future.

items.def: A unit of ownership in a company
A share of profit paid to shareholders
Share price × number of shares
First sale of shares to the public

blocks.latex: Market cap = Share price × Shares outstanding

blocks.q: If a share is 200 and there are 1,000,000 shares, market cap is…

lessons.title: Exchanges & Indices
lessons.summary: Where stocks trade and how we measure them.

blocks.text: Exchanges & Indices
Stocks trade on exchanges like the NSE and BSE. An index such as the Nifty 50 or Sensex tracks a basket of large companies to summarise the market's direction.

items.def: Marketplace where shares are bought and sold
A basket of stocks tracked as one number
Index of 50 large Indian companies
Index of 30 large BSE companies

blocks.back: A fund that simply mirrors an index like the Nifty 50

lessons.title: Order Types
lessons.summary: Market, limit, stop — say what you mean.

blocks.text: Order Types
How you place an order controls the price you get and the risk you take.

rows: Buy/sell now at the best available price
Execute only at your price or better
Trigger a sell if price falls to a level

blocks.text: Use limit orders for illiquid stocks so you don't get a nasty fill.
blocks.title: Pro tip

opts: Your price or better, but not execution
items.explain: Limit orders control price, not certainty of filling.

blocks.text: Mutual Funds 101
A mutual fund pools money from many investors and a manager invests it according to a stated strategy. You buy units; their value is the NAV (net asset value).

items.def: Per-unit value of the fund
Total assets the fund manages
Annual fee as a % of your investment
Fee for selling within a set period

blocks.text: Fees compound against you. A 1% higher expense ratio can cost lakhs over decades.
blocks.title: Watch fees

blocks.explain: Net Asset Value, the per-unit price.

blocks.text: Index Funds & ETFs
Index funds and ETFs aim to match an index rather than beat it. They charge tiny fees and, over the long run, beat most active managers precisely because of those low costs.

items: Index funds match the market at very low cost
ETFs trade like stocks during market hours
Most active funds underperform their index after fees

items.q: ETF vs index fund — what's the difference?
items.a: Both track an index. ETFs trade intraday like stocks; index mutual funds transact once daily at NAV.
Yes — and that's the point. Boring and cheap usually wins.

items.q: Why do index funds often beat active funds long term?
items.explain: Low costs compound in your favour.

blocks.text: Good Debt vs Bad Debt
Good debt helps you build wealth or income (a reasonable home loan, education). Bad debt funds depreciating wants at high interest (credit-card revolving balances, payday loans).
Credit-card interest at ~40% will out-run almost any investment. Clear it first.
blocks.title: Priority

blocks.explain: Its very high interest erodes wealth fast.

blocks.text: Credit Scores
A credit score (like CIBIL, 300–900) predicts how reliably you repay. A higher score unlocks lower interest rates and faster approvals.

items: Pay every bill on time — payment history matters most
Keep credit utilisation below 30%
Don't close your oldest card; length of history helps

items.def: Balance owed ÷ total credit limit
A lender checking your score for a new loan
Age of your credit accounts

items.explain: Under 30% signals you're not over-reliant on credit.

items.q: The biggest driver of a credit score is…
items.explain: Consistently paying on time matters most.

blocks.text: Avalanche vs Snowball
Both methods pay minimums on everything, then attack one debt with extra cash.
Avalanche is mathematically cheaper; snowball is psychologically easier. The best method is the one you'll stick to.

blocks.back: Pay highest-interest debt first to minimise total interest

lessons.title: Start Early: The Cost of Waiting

blocks.text: Start Early: The Cost of Waiting
Because of compounding, money invested in your 20s does far more heavy lifting than money invested later — even if the later amount is much larger.
Anya invested for 10 years and stopped; Riya invested for 25 years. Anya often still wins — time beats amount.
blocks.title: Key lesson

blocks.q: The biggest advantage of investing early is…

blocks.text: Retirement Accounts
Dedicated accounts give tax breaks for locking money up until retirement. In India the common ones are EPF, PPF, and NPS.

items.def: Employer + employee retirement contribution
15-year govt-backed tax-free savings
Market-linked national pension scheme
When employer contributions become yours

blocks.text: How Much Do You Need?
A common target: save 25× your annual expenses, then withdraw about 4% per year. This 'financial independence' number scales with your lifestyle, not your income.

blocks.q: If you spend 6,00,000 a year, your rough FI number is…

modules.title: Behavioral Finance
modules.subtitle: Master the investor in the mirror

blocks.text: Common Biases
Most investing mistakes are emotional, not analytical. Naming your biases is the first step to beating them.

items.def: Losses hurt about twice as much as gains feel good
Over-weighting what just happened
Following the crowd into bubbles
Seeking info that agrees with you
Fixating on an irrelevant reference price
Buying out of fear of missing out

items.q: Selling in a panic crash is driven mostly by…
items.explain: Fear of further loss plus crowd behaviour.

items.q: Buying a hot stock only because it doubled last month is…

blocks.text: Time in the Market > Timing the Market
Missing just a handful of the market's best days — which often cluster right after the worst days — can devastate long-term returns. Staying invested usually beats jumping in and out.
Investors who panic-sell crashes tend to also miss the rebounds. The recovery often comes fast.
blocks.title: The trap

blocks.back: Time IN the market beats TIMING the market

blocks.q: Why is market timing so dangerous?
opts: Best days often follow worst days
blocks.explain: Miss the rebound and your returns collapse.

modules.title: Taxes for Investors
modules.subtitle: Keep more of what you earn

blocks.text: Capital Gains Basics
A capital gain is profit from selling an asset for more than you paid. How long you held it usually changes the tax rate — long-term holding is generally taxed more gently.

items.def: What you originally paid, incl. charges
Short-term capital gain (shorter holding)
Long-term capital gain (longer holding)
Profit locked in once you sell

blocks.text: You're typically taxed only when you SELL (realise the gain). Unrealised gains keep compounding untaxed.
blocks.title: Key idea

blocks.q: You're generally taxed on a capital gain when you…

lessons.title: Tax-Smart Habits
lessons.summary: Simple, legal ways to pay less.

blocks.text: Tax-Smart Habits

items: Use tax-advantaged accounts (PPF, NPS, ELSS) first
Hold long enough to qualify for lower long-term rates
Harvest losses to offset gains where allowed
Keep clean records of cost basis and charges

blocks.text: Never let the tax tail wag the investment dog — a good investment with some tax beats a bad one with none.

blocks.back: Selling losers to offset taxable gains

blocks.text: Moving Averages & RSI
A moving average smooths price to reveal the trend. The RSI (Relative Strength Index) ranges 0–100 and hints at overbought (>70) or oversold (<30) conditions.
Indicators are hints, not guarantees. They work best together and with risk management.
blocks.title: Reality check

blocks.explain: Above 70 is the classic overbought zone.
